synopsis: Brake dead time runs from brake command to the first braking effect, while build-up time continues until full braking force; ISO 3450 stopping distance includes both but excludes operator reaction time [f13664, f13674, f5976]. At 5–15 km/h, latency can account for half or more of stopping distance, and a half-second error in assumed dead time causes about 2 m of stopping-distance error at 15 km/h [f5898, f13682]. Published architecture-specific examples include under 0.3 s for a 2026 tracked-vehicle electro-hydraulic brake, 0.41 s for a 2025 mining electric vehicle brake-by-wire system, and historic retarder lags of 1–2 s; MSHA instead prescribes weight-class response assumptions of 0.5–2.5 s plus one second of operator time [f5893, f5894, f5897, f6053, f6058]. Queensland's two-second, 22.2 m delay example at 40 km/h combines operator reaction and mechanical delay, so it is not a measured automatic-brake response [f3220]. Modern production-loader, articulated-hauler and haul-truck delay distributions were not found, so prototype testing should measure the automated braking path before large scenario sweeps and characterize timing variability as well as average delay [f13683, f13684, f12573, f13678, f13680]. The recommended core is a calibrated point-mass stopping model with measured latency, build-up lag and worst-case deceleration by grade, payload and surface, validated against the full detection-to-position timing chain rather than minimum stopping distance alone [f146, f7786].
